chapter: Jelly Roll's road trip, Benny Carter and Chick Webb
title: Developing his tone: records, Jeff's lead, and Jimmy Dorsey's list
summary: He explains how he learned from records, how Hilton Jefferson's tone won the lead chair in Webb's section, and that Jimmy Dorsey named him among the twelve best alto players.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: How was your own playing developing at this point? Had you changed? Were you constantly changing at that time? Were you --
You were getting better and better.
Well, I hope I was, anyway.
But had anything -- had you heard things that were influencing your style?
Oh, of course, sure. I used to -- you

know, I think I told how I used to buy records, everybody's records, you know. If something came out I'd buy it and then during the day, you know, I'd play these records and listen to them, and -- because that was the only way you could pick up on what was happening, you know. I'd buy all the stuff. I bought Paul Whiteman's records, Ben Bernie's records, and then I got to know all those fellows later on and it was -- it was fine. There were a lot of people -- you see, then you'd listen to this man for one thing, you'd listen to this other, you'd listen to him to hear his technique, then you'd listen to this one. In those days you used to call it his tone. They don't talk about tone anymore, because however you sound, you could honk on it, and if you're honking, well, that's good enough.

But in those days if you were a saxophone player you had to play with some kind of tone. You had to have some beauty in your playing, like they say, and if you didn't have it, then you were kaput. Like I remember in Chick Webb's band we had the three saxophone players, Elmer Williams, Hilton Jefferson and myself, and we used to alternate on the playing the lead, you know, because Jeff had a better tone than I did. See, he could play something real pretty and beautiful. So he played the first part, you know. But later on I developed some sort of a tone. I don't know how good it was. But -- and -- well, I think I must have developed it pretty good, because during

the time I was in Chicago with Kirby, Jimmy Dorsey -- of course I knew him, he used to come around. He's a fun guy. He's a happy guy. He used to come around, and he wrote a magazine article. I don't think that magazine is still existing. He wrote a magazine article and he picked the 12 best alto players, and he picked me as one of them, which I thought was a terrific thing, you know, and I meant to keep that magazine, but I've long since lost it. I don't know what happened to it. And it had all our pictures, of the 12. He picked the 12 best. So I guess I did improve a little bit.
